seo_title: What Happens If Appraisers Disagree? The Umpire Process
meta_description: What happens if appraisers disagree? How disputed items go to an umpire, how the award is signed, and what Texas owners can do.
h1: What Happens If Appraisers Disagree During an Insurance Appraisal?
excerpt: When the two appraisers cannot agree on the amount of loss, the disputed items go to a neutral umpire. Learn how that works, how the award is signed, and how to strengthen your position.
key_takeaways: When appraisers disagree, the disputed items are submitted to a neutral umpire.
Appraisers often agree on most items and send only a few to the umpire.
An award signed by any two of the three panel members sets the amount.
If appraisers cannot agree on an umpire, a court can usually appoint one.
Strong, item-by-item evidence is what persuades an umpire.
body_html:
If appraisers disagree on the amount of loss, the items they cannot settle are submitted to a neutral umpire. The umpire reviews both appraisers' estimates and evidence, may inspect the property, and decides each disputed item. An award signed by the umpire and one appraiser, or by both appraisers, generally sets the amount of loss.

Why do insurance appraisers disagree?

Disagreement is built into the appraisal process. Each party selects its own appraiser, and each appraiser looks at the damage, the evidence, and the repair method from a different starting point. Honest professionals can reach different conclusions about the same roof or room.

The most common sources of disagreement on Texas property claims include:

  • Scope: whether a roof, siding, or flooring should be replaced or repaired
  • Causation: whether damage came from the storm or from age, wear, or a prior event
  • Quantities: roof squares, pitch, waste, linear feet of flashing, and room measurements
  • Pricing: material and labor costs, steep and high-roof charges, and overhead and profit
  • Code items: whether upgrades are required by local building codes
  • Matching: whether undamaged areas must be replaced to achieve a reasonably uniform appearance
  • Depreciation: how much to deduct for age and condition

Knowing what happens if appraisers disagree helps you prepare for it. When you understand which issues are likely to be contested on your claim, you can gather the right evidence early instead of scrambling after the umpire is involved.

None of these disagreements means the process has failed. Appraisal is designed to resolve exactly these kinds of differences.

Do appraisers have to agree on everything?

No. In most appraisals, the appraisers agree on many items and disagree on a few. A typical approach is to go through the estimates line by line, settle what they can, and list the remaining disputed items separately.

For example, two appraisers might quickly agree on interior paint, gutters, and fence repairs, but disagree on whether the entire roof needs replacement and on the waste factor. Only those two issues would go to the umpire.

An illustrative example

Imagine a hail claim where the policyholder's appraiser values the loss at $38,000 and the insurer's appraiser values it at $21,000. After working through the estimates together, they agree on $17,000 of interior, gutter, and fence items. The remaining gap comes down to two issues:

  • Full roof replacement versus repair of two slopes
  • A 10% versus 15% waste factor on a complex hip roof

The umpire would decide only those two issues. If the umpire finds full replacement is supported but the lower waste factor is correct, the award reflects both decisions, and whichever appraiser agrees signs it with the umpire.

This partial agreement saves time and money. The fewer items the umpire must decide, the faster and less expensive the process usually is.

How does the umpire resolve the disagreement?

Most policies require the appraisers to select an umpire at the beginning of the process, so one is ready if needed. When disagreement remains, the umpire steps in. A common sequence looks like this:

StageWhat happens
SubmissionAppraisers send the umpire agreed and disputed items, estimates, and supporting evidence.
ReviewThe umpire studies photos, measurement reports, engineering reports, and code references.
InspectionThe umpire may inspect the property, often with both appraisers present.
PresentationEach appraiser explains its position on each disputed item.
DecisionThe umpire decides each item and signs the award with the appraiser who agrees.

The umpire is not required to split the difference. On each item, the umpire weighs the evidence and may side fully with one appraiser, fully with the other, or land somewhere in between. Learn more about the role in what an insurance umpire does. In most cases, the umpire's decision ends the disagreement.

What if the appraisers cannot agree on an umpire?

Sometimes the disagreement starts earlier, when the appraisers cannot agree on who the umpire should be. Most Texas policies give the appraisers a set number of days, often 15, to choose one.

If they cannot agree, either party can usually ask a court in the county where the property is located to appoint an umpire. Court appointment adds time and expense, but it keeps the process moving. Our guide on how insurance umpires are chosen in Texas explains the options in more detail.

A related situation is an impasse, where the process stalls because appraisers stop responding, refuse to engage, or reach a deadlock without a functioning umpire. Read what an impasse in insurance appraisal is for how those situations are typically handled.

Delays at this stage are frustrating, but they are rarely permanent. Document every request your appraiser sends and every response, or lack of one. If a court ultimately has to appoint an umpire or address a stalled appraisal, that written record shows who tried to move the process forward and when.

How is the appraisal award signed when appraisers disagree?

Most appraisal clauses provide that a written award agreed to by any two of the three panel members sets the amount of loss. That leads to three possible outcomes:

  1. Both appraisers agree. They sign the award together, and the umpire does not need to decide anything.
  2. The umpire agrees with the policyholder's appraiser. Those two sign the award.
  3. The umpire agrees with the insurer's appraiser. Those two sign the award.

When the umpire decides items differently from both appraisers, the umpire typically issues an award that one appraiser is willing to sign. Either way, the award carries the same weight. The final award often itemizes replacement cost, depreciation, and actual cash value, and it may separate dwelling, other structures, and contents.

Tip: Ask your appraiser for a copy of the final award and the itemized breakdown. You need those details to understand your payment and to recover depreciation after repairs on a replacement cost policy.

What persuades an umpire when appraisers disagree?

The umpire only sees what the appraisers present. The appraiser with clear, specific, item-by-item support generally has the advantage. Helpful evidence includes:

  • Close-up and overview photos tied to specific roof slopes, elevations, and rooms
  • Measurement reports, roof diagrams, and room dimensions
  • Test square results, brittleness tests, and manufacturer information for roofing disputes
  • Moisture readings and timelines for interior damage
  • Building department letters and code references for required upgrades
  • Local supplier quotes and invoices for pricing disputes
  • 3D documentation, such as Matterport scans, showing conditions before repairs

What weakens an appraiser's position

Some approaches tend to backfire in front of an umpire:

  • Lump-sum numbers without line-item support
  • Photos that cannot be tied to a specific location on the property
  • Pricing that does not reflect the local market
  • Claiming items that were clearly not damaged by the covered event

Overreaching on a few items can cast doubt on an otherwise solid estimate. A disciplined, well-documented position usually serves the policyholder better.

See our complete guide to what evidence helps during insurance appraisal.

Appraiser disagreements on Texas claims

Texas policyholders file a large number of hail and wind claims, from Lubbock and Amarillo to Dallas-Fort Worth, Waco, and Austin, plus hurricane claims along the Gulf Coast. Disagreements in these appraisals frequently focus on roof replacement, hail versus wear and tear, and storm-related interior leaks.

Under State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (Tex. 2009), appraisers and umpires in Texas may decide the amount of loss and consider whether damage was caused by the covered event, but they do not decide coverage. If the real disagreement is about whether the policy covers the loss, that question is resolved outside appraisal.

Texas courts generally enforce appraisal awards and set them aside only in limited situations, such as fraud, accident, or mistake. After an award, payment timing is governed by the policy and Texas Insurance Code Chapter 542. If you are considering legal options after appraisal, our article on whether you can sue after insurance appraisal covers the basics. This is general information, not legal advice.

How long does it take to resolve a disagreement?

It depends on how many items are disputed, the size of the loss, how quickly the umpire can inspect, and the availability of everyone involved. Many residential disputes are resolved within weeks of being submitted to the umpire. Large or commercial losses with many disputed items and multiple inspections can take longer.

You can keep the process moving by responding quickly to information requests, providing access to the property, and giving your appraiser complete documentation from the start. For a stage-by-stage overview, see our insurance appraisal timeline.

Next steps if your appraisers disagree

Disagreement between appraisers is normal, and it is not a sign that your claim is in trouble. In many appraisals, the umpire stage is simply the last step before the award, and it often focuses on a small number of items. What matters is how well each side's position is supported when the dispute reaches the umpire.

If your claim is already in appraisal and the appraisers are far apart, you can help by:

  1. Giving your appraiser every photo, estimate, invoice, and letter you have
  2. Writing down when you first noticed each area of damage
  3. Providing access to the property for umpire inspections
  4. Avoiding direct contact with the umpire or the insurer's appraiser about the amount of loss

faqs.q: Does the umpire always split the difference between appraisers?
faqs.a: No. An umpire decides each disputed item on its merits and the evidence presented. On some items the umpire may side fully with one appraiser, and on others land in between. Appraisers who present inflated or unsupported numbers often lose credibility, while well-documented positions tend to carry more weight with the umpire.

faqs.q: Can I reject the award if the umpire sides with the insurer?
faqs.a: Generally, an award signed by two of the three panel members binds both parties on the amount of loss, even if you disagree with the outcome. Texas courts set aside awards only in narrow circumstances, such as fraud, accident, mistake, or failure to follow the policy. Talk with an attorney if you believe one of those applies.

faqs.q: What if my appraiser and the insurer's appraiser stop communicating?
faqs.a: If communication breaks down, the process can stall. Your appraiser can submit disputed items to the umpire, and if no umpire has been selected, either party can usually ask a court to appoint one. Keep written records of attempts to move the process forward, as they help if a court needs to get involved.

faqs.q: Does it cost more when appraisers disagree?
faqs.a: It can. Under most Texas policies, each side pays its own appraiser, and the parties split the umpire's fees. When more items go to the umpire, umpire costs usually rise. Narrowing the dispute to a short list of well-defined items helps control cost. An appraisal cost calculator can help you weigh costs against likely recovery.

faqs.q: Can the umpire decide whether damage is covered by my policy?
faqs.a: No. In Texas, appraisers and umpires decide the amount of loss and may consider the extent of damage and whether it was caused by the covered event. Whether the policy covers a loss, or whether an exclusion applies, is a coverage question that falls outside appraisal and may need to be resolved separately.
